fatal_errors: The proposed baseline of a linear decrease in modulus and hardness contradicts the stated increase in elastic modulus at 600 K.
Localized amorphization is asserted as the decisive mechanism without evidence distinguishing amorphous atoms from generic thermally disordered or highly strained FCC atoms.
Stacking-fault annihilation is not reconciled with the target trend of increasing HCP atom count with temperature, since HCP classifications commonly represent stacking-fault environments.
Changing the potential or reducing indentation velocity strongly alters stacking-fault energetics and strain-rate response, so the proposed controls do not isolate disorder from mechanical annealing.
explanation: The hypothesis correctly identifies the material system, indentation depth and velocity, temperature series, approximately 900 K transition, dislocation reduction, lattice disorder, friction fluctuations, and loss of hardness and wear resistance. It also proposes relevant observables—HCP/FCC/disordered atom populations, dislocation line length, friction, and hardness. However, it replaces the target's broader lattice-disorder mechanism with an unsupported mandatory sequence of Shockley-partial annihilation, dislocation starvation, and interfacial amorphization. Its baseline misses the anomalous modulus increase at 600 K, and important simulation conditions such as geometry, orientation, boundary conditions, thermostat regions, ensemble, and unloading are omitted. A cleaner falsification would use otherwise identical trajectories at each temperature and compare time-resolved HCP count, PTM/CNA disorder fraction, and dislocation line length before loading, at maximum depth, and after unloading: persistent disorder accompanied by friction increase would support thermal disorder, whereas recovery of HCP defects and reduced line length during unloading without growth of noncrystalline atoms would support mechanical annealing.
